analysis.one_liner: Requires large warehouses to disclose work quotas, provide paid breaks, and limit worker surveillance.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2025 with 21 cosponsors including one Republican, the bill has sat in two House committees with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets large warehouse employers — operations with more than 200 workers in warehousing, wholesaling, online retail fulfillment, or courier work. It would require those employers to give workers a written description of every work quota, including any discipline tied to it and what monitoring technology is used; bar quotas that cut into legally required breaks, bathroom use, or accommodations; give workers a paid 15-minute break for every four hours worked; let workers see, dispute, and correct the speed data collected on them; and add new workplace safety rules, including an ergonomics standard to prevent muscle and joint injuries and faster medical referrals after injuries. It would be enforced by the Labor Department and the FTC, with penalties up to $76,987 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse workers subject to productivity quotas — an estimated large share of the nation's warehouse workforce, including at the biggest e-commerce fulfillment operations. They would gain the right to know their quotas in writing, see and challenge the speed data used against them, take paid rest breaks without losing quota credit, and get faster medical care after injuries. Labor unions and worker advocacy groups would also gain formal roles in inspections and complaint filing.

how_it_helps.text: Covered employers must give each worker a written description of every quota: the number of tasks required, any discipline for missing it, how the target is calculated, and what surveillance technology collects speed data on them [S2].

Employers may not impose quotas that prevent legally required breaks, bathroom use (including travel time), safety compliance, or workplace accommodations, and may not discipline workers for missing quotas that were never disclosed or that rank them against coworkers [S2].
Workers get a paid 15-minute rest break for every four hours worked, plus notice and posted signage of that right in their primary language [S2].

Workers can request their own speed data and the aggregated data for coworkers in plain language, ask for corrections, and record why time went unworked — including bathroom trips, injury reporting, or union activity — with employers required to revisit any discipline based on corrected data [S2].

The Labor Department must investigate any covered employer whose injury rate is at least 1.5 times the warehousing industry average, or that draws five credible worker complaints in a year, and union or worker-advocacy representatives can join inspections [S2].

Retaliation within 90 days of a worker asserting these rights creates a presumption of illegal retaliation, and pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers would not apply to claims under the bill [S2].
OSHA would have to write a first-ever ergonomics standard for warehouse work to prevent musculoskeletal injuries, and a standard requiring prompt first aid and medical referral after injuries [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large warehouse operators — warehousing and storage firms, wholesalers, online retail fulfillment centers, and couriers with over 200 employees, including staffing agencies supplying them. They would bear compliance costs: written quota disclosures, paid breaks, data access and correction systems, recordkeeping, civil penalties up to $76,987 per violation (up to $769,870 for willful or repeat violations), and new OSHA safety standards. Workplace surveillance technology vendors would lose sales where data-minimization rules limit their products.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large warehouse and e-commerce logistics employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly: written quota disclosures, paid 15-minute breaks every four hours, data access and correction systems, three-year recordkeeping, and penalties up to $769,870 for willful violations [S2]. Employers near the 200-employee threshold face the same burden as the largest operators.

The bill extends FTC consumer-protection enforcement to workplace rules and lets any worker designate an outside advocacy organization to file complaints and join inspections, which employers would argue invites excessive litigation and agency overreach [S2].

The mandated OSHA ergonomics standard — a rulemaking OSHA last attempted in 2000 before Congress blocked it — would be a heavy regulatory lift with a 3-year deadline, and its costs would fall on operators in a thin-margin industry [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that paid breaks and slower quota discipline could raise costs that employers pass on through lower starting pay, fewer hours, or automation — effects the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in an industry with among the highest injury rates in the country, the transparency, break, and medical-referral provisions address documented, specific harms: undisclosed quotas, speed data used to discipline workers without their ever seeing it, and pressure that discourages bathroom breaks and injury reporting. The costs are real — compliance burdens, potential pay or automation effects, and an aggressive multi-agency enforcement design — but they fall on employers of a scale (200+ employees) that can absorb them. The main design weakness is relying on rulemakings and a new Labor Department office that depend on future administrations funding and pursuing them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on August 5, 2025 and referred to two House committees — Education and Workforce, and Energy and Commerce — where it has received no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross (D-NJ) introduced the Warehouse Worker Protection Act on August 5, 2025 with 12 original cosponsors, including one Republican [S2].
The Speaker assigned it to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, each for the provisions in its jurisdiction [S4].
The bill has 21 cosponsors: 20 House Democrats and 1 House Republican [S3].
As of the latest action record, neither committee has held a hearing or markup, and the House has not voted on the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: large warehouse operators continue operating under the current quota and surveillance rules with no compliance costs, and the bill's beneficiaries — quota-track warehouse workers — have gained nothing yet. With no committee action and a narrow House majority, the likely path is the same as most single-sponsor labor bills: it expires at the end of the Congress without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors but one are Democrats; the single Republican original cosponsor (Rep. Lawler) is the exception, and no committee action has occurred under the Republican House majority.

industries.industry: Large warehouse and e-commerce logistics operators (warehousing, wholesaling, online fulfillment, couriers with 200+ employees)
industries.note: The bill directly regulates how these employers set quotas, monitor workers, handle breaks, and manage injuries, with civil penalties up to $769,870 for willful violations. The costs they would bear are the protections workers would gain, so their interest in stopping the bill runs against the workers it covers.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and productivity-tracking technology vendors
industries.note: The bill requires disclosure of surveillance tools, restricts data collection to what is strictly necessary to track quota compliance, and gives workers access to and correction of their speed data — narrowing the market for continuous-monitoring products sold to warehouse operators.

industries.industry: Staffing and temporary-worker agencies serving large warehouses
industries.note: The bill explicitly covers staffing agencies, temp firms, and contractor arrangements as covered employers, so they face the same quota-disclosure, break, and recordkeeping duties as direct employers. Some agency workers gain new protections; agencies bear compliance costs and lose flexibility in how they place and manage quota-track labor.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill gives these groups statutory roles: accompanying Labor Department inspections (even at a worker's anonymous request), filing complaints on behalf of workers, joining settlement negotiations, and serving on a Quota Task Force to help enforce the law.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in two committees with no scheduled hearing, 21 cosponsors, and a narrow House majority. A single-sponsor labor bill at this stage, in a divided Congress, very rarely reaches the floor; the most likely path is that it receives no committee action and expires at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027, though a hearing or a companion Senate bill could extend its life.
